label: Book III. Wherein Christ is shown to be the Son of God, Who created the world; to have been predicted by the prophets; to have taken human flesh like our own, by a real incarnation. — Marcion's Christ Not the Subject of Prophecy. The Absurd Consequences of This Theory of the Heretic.
context: Book III. Wherein Christ is shown to be the Son of God, Who created the world; to have been predicted by the prophets; to have taken human flesh like our own, by a real incarnation.

blocks.text: Chapter IV.—Marcion’s Christ Not the Subject of Prophecy. The Absurd Consequences of This Theory of the Heretic.

He [^tertullian-against-marcion-v-iv-814] disdained, I suppose, to imitate the order of our God, as one who was displeasing to him, and was by all means to be vanquished. He wished to come, as a new being in a new way—a son previous to his father’s announcement, a sent one before the authority of the sender; so that he might in person [^tertullian-against-marcion-v-iv-815] propagate a most monstrous faith, whereby it should come to be believed that Christ was come before it should be known that He had an existence. It is here convenient to me to treat that other point: Why he came not after Christ? For when I observe that, during so long a period, his lord [^tertullian-against-marcion-v-iv-816] bore with the greatest patience the very ruthless Creator who was all the while announcing His Christ to men, I say, that whatever reason impelled him to do so, postponing thereby his own revelation and interposition, the self-same reason imposed on him the duty of bearing with the Creator (who had also in His Christ dispensations of His own to carry out); so that, after the completion and accomplishment of the entire plan of the rival God and the rival Christ, [^tertullian-against-marcion-v-iv-817] he might then superinduce his own proper dispensation. But he grew weary of so long an endurance, and so failed to wait till the end of the Creator’s course. It was of no use, his enduring that his Christ should be predicted, when he refused to permit him to be manifested. [^tertullian-against-marcion-v-iv-818] Either it was without just cause that he interrupted the full course of his rival’s time, or without just cause did he so long refrain from interrupting it. What held him back at first? Or what disturbed him at last? As the case now stands, however, [^tertullian-against-marcion-v-iv-819] he has committed himself in respect of both, having revealed himself so tardily after the Creator, so hurriedly before His Christ; whereas he ought long ago to have encountered the one with a confutation, the other to have forborne encountering as yet—not to have borne with the one so long in His ruthless hostility, nor to have disquieted the other, who was as yet quiescent! In the case of both, while depriving them of their title to be considered the most good God, he showed himself at least capricious and uncertain; lukewarm (in his resentment) towards the Creator, but fervid against His Christ, and powerless [^tertullian-against-marcion-v-iv-820] in respect of them both! For he no more restrained the Creator than he resisted His Christ. The Creator still remains such as He really is. His Christ also will come, [^tertullian-against-marcion-v-iv-821] just as it is written of Him. Why did he [^tertullian-against-marcion-v-iv-822] come after the Creator, since he was unable to correct Him by punishment? [^tertullian-against-marcion-v-iv-823] Why did he reveal himself before Christ, whom he could not hinder from appearing? [^tertullian-against-marcion-v-iv-824] If, on the contrary, [^tertullian-against-marcion-v-iv-825] he did chastise the Creator, he revealed himself, (I suppose,) after Him in order that things which require correction might come first. On which account also, (of course,) he ought to have waited for Christ to appear first, whom he was going to chastise in like manner; then he would be His punisher coming after Him, [^tertullian-against-marcion-v-iv-826] just as he had been in the case of the Creator. There is another consideration: since he will at his second advent come after Him, that as he at His first coming took hostile proceedings against the Creator, destroying the law and the prophets, which were His, so he may, to be sure, [^tertullian-against-marcion-v-iv-827] at his second coming proceed in opposition to Christ, upsetting [^tertullian-against-marcion-v-iv-828] His kingdom. Then, no doubt, he would terminate his course, and then (if ever) [^tertullian-against-marcion-v-iv-829] be worthy of belief; for else, if his work has been already perfected, it would be in vain for him to come, for there would indeed be nothing that he could further accomplish.

tertullian-against-marcion-v-iv-816.text: Ejus (i.e. Marcionis) Dominum, meaning Marcion’s God, who had not yet been revealed.

tertullian-against-marcion-v-iv-817.text: The Creator and His Christ, as rivals of Marcion’s.

tertullian-against-marcion-v-iv-818.text: He twits Marcion with introducing his Christ on the scene too soon . He ought to have waited until the Creator’s Christ (prophesied of through the Old Testament) had come. Why allow him to be predicted, and then forbid His actual coming, by his own arrival on the scene first? Of course, M. must be understood to deny that the Christ of the New Testament is the subject of the Old Testament prophecies at all. Hence T.’s anxiety to adduce prophecy as the main evidence of our Lord as being really the Creator’s Christ.

tertullian-against-marcion-v-iv-821.text: The reader will remember that Tertullian is here arguing on Marcion’s ground, according to whom the Creator’s Christ, the Christ predicted through the O.T., was yet to come. Marcion’s Christ, however, had proved himself so weak to stem the Creator’s course, that he had no means really of checking the Creator’s Christ from coming. It had been better, adds Tertullian, if Marcion’s Christ had waited for the Creator’s Christ to have first appeared.

tertullian-against-marcion-v-iv-826.text: Posterior emendator futurus: an instance of Tertullian’s style in paradox.
